description:
TTCodersStudio is an innovative software team turning complex NASA space data into high-performance, user-centric digital solutions through agile problem-solving and creative data sonification.

TTCodersStudio, TTCS, NASA Space Apps Challenge Team, data analysis, open-source space data solutions, Denizli
summary: AeroJukebox is an accessible web app that turns real-time NASA and atmospheric data into a living tree, real-time music, and voice narration. Users can explore three global map modes—Air Quality (Open-Meteo & NASA POWER), Wildfire Risk (live NASA EONET active fires), and Light Pollution (NASA GIBS VIIRS night lights)—plus a 1750–2026 historical time slider. Instead of showing only complex charts, a dynamic tree reacts to the environment (changing across 5 health stages, catching fire during wildfires, or glowing with stars and fireflies at night) while our Web Audio API engine translates the data into comfortable, emotional music. With 5-language support, full keyboard control, voice reading, an interactive Spotlight Guide, and CosmoAI (Google Gemini), AeroJukebox lets everyone—including blind and low-vision users—hear and feel how our planet is doing.
details:
NASA’s Earth Information Center shares great data and visuals about our planet, but almost all of it is only for people who can see. For the “The Earth Information Jukebox” challenge, our team wanted to change that. We asked: how can a blind person, or someone who finds big data tables hard to read, understand what is happening in our atmosphere? That is why we created AeroJukebox a web app that turns real-time NASA satellite data into a living tree, real-time music, and spoken explanations.

AeroJukebox works directly in any web browser, on both computers and phones, and you do not need to install anything. You can click anywhere on the world map, search for a city, or use quick station buttons. The app has three different map modes:

  1. Air Quality: Shows live air pollution data (PM2.5, PM10, NO₂, O₃, CO, AQI), temperature, and humidity from Open-Meteo (Copernicus CAMS), plus solar radiation data from NASA POWER.
  2. Wildfire Risk: Works separately from air quality. It shows real active wildfires from NASA EONET on the map and calculates fire risk from temperature, dry air, and dust.
  3. Light Pollution: Uses NASA GIBS VIIRS Black Marble night-lights data on the map to show how bright the night sky is (Bortle Scale 1–9).
    There is also a 1750–2026 Time Slider so you can compare clean air before factories with today’s levels.

Instead of only showing numbers, our app turns this data into visuals and sound at the same time. On the right side, an HTML5 Canvas draws a moving tree in real time. In Air Quality mode, the tree changes across 5 stages—from a bright green tree with flowers and oxygen bubbles to yellow falling leaves, and finally a dry, bare tree in heavy smog. In Wildfire mode, if the fire risk is high, the tree actually catches fire with moving flames and flying sparks. In Light Pollution mode, a dark sky shows stars and fireflies, while a bright city hides the stars and adds streetlamp glare with moths.

At the same time, our Web Audio API sound system plays live music for every situation. Clean air plays calm, happy chords and soft bells. Medium pollution changes into sad, slower notes. Heavy pollution plays a deep, heavy bass sound with a soft warning pulse. Wildfires play fire crackle sounds, and light-polluted cities play a low neon city hum.

One important thing our team thought about was how the bad air sounds. If you turn raw numbers directly into sound, it makes a harsh noise that hurts your ears. We worked carefully on the musical scales and audio compressor so that polluted air and wildfires clearly sound serious and sad, but still stay comfortable to listen to. We also focused strongly on accessibility for blind and low-vision users. Because clicking a map is hard without seeing, users can search cities, use quick buttons, control everything with the keyboard (Space, F, V, R, M, H, and arrow keys), switch between Dark and Light themes, and listen to a 5-language voice reader (English, Turkish, German, French, and Czech). We even added a step-by-step Spotlight Guide for new users and CosmoAI (powered by Google Gemini, with an offline backup), which reads the live data of your chosen spot and answers your questions simply.

We built AeroJukebox using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript with Leaflet.js for the map and Esri ArcGIS simple base maps. We tested it on our laptops, tablets, and phones with headphones. We also added backup data models so the app keeps working smoothly even if an internet API is slow.

Our goal is simple: we want people not just to look at Earth science, but to actually hear and feel how our planet is doing—no matter where they are or whether they can see the screen.
